en: The *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra* (Treatise on Entering Logic), one fascicle.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Śaṅkarasvāmin;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.
The proof and the refutation, as well as their fallacious counterparts, serve solely to enlighten others;
direct perception and inference, along with their fallacious counterparts, serve solely for one’s own enlightenment.
Thus, these summarize the essential points of all treatises.
In this context, the multiple statements consisting of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth are termed the "proof" (*sādhana*).
This is because the multiple statements of the thesis, reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) reveal the meaning that has not yet been understood by those who inquire.

In this context, the "thesis" (pakṣa) refers to a subject that is generally accepted, which has as its nature a qualifier that is also generally accepted, and which is intended by oneself to be established; this is called the thesis.
For example, in establishing that "sound is impermanent," there are three characteristics of the reason (*hetu*).
What are these three?

That is to say: the property of being entirely present in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), the property of being necessarily present in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and the property of being entirely absent in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*).
What are called "similar instances" (*sapakṣa*) and "dissimilar instances" (*vipakṣa*)?
Those things which share the same logical status as the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*) are called "similar instances."
For example, when "impermanence" is established, such that jars and the like are impermanent, these are called similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

As for dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), they refer to cases where that which is to be established is absent, such as: "If something is permanent, it is seen to be non-produced, like space and so forth."

In this context, the property of being produced by effort (*kṛtakatva*) or the property of being originated by uninterrupted application of effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*).

The "necessary presence in similar instances" (*sapakṣe sattvam*) and the "complete absence from dissimilar instances" (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*) constitute the reasons for [the property of] impermanence and so forth.
There are two kinds of analogies:
first, the analogy of similarity;
second, the analogy of dissimilarity.
The "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) is that wherein it is shown that the reason is definitely present in similar cases; for example: "Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, such as a jar."

The dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*) is where, in a given case, the probandum is stated to be absent and the reason is universally non-existent; for example: "If it were eternal, it would be seen to be unproduced, like space and so forth."

In this context, the term "permanent" indicates "not impermanent," and the term "uncreated" indicates "that which is not produced. Just as that which is not existent is called "non-existent," so it is here.
It has been stated that when such numerous statements, including the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth, are employed to enlighten others, they are termed "proof" (*sādhana*).
For example, the statement "Sound is impermanent" is the expression of the thesis.
"Because it is a product" is the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
"If it is a product, it is seen to be impermanent, like a jar and so forth" is the statement of the concordant instance (*sapakṣa*).
"If it were eternal, its being seen would not be produced, like space"—this is the exclusion of speech (*vacanavyavaccheda*).
Only these three members are called the "proof" (*sādhana*).
Although it may be intended as a valid establishment, because it contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge, it is called a "pseudo-proposition" (*pratijñābhāsa*).

These are: contradiction with direct perception, contradiction with inference (*anumāna*), contradiction with one's own scriptures, contradiction with worldly consensus, contradiction with one's own words, non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-asiddha*), non-establishment of the qualificand (*viśeṣya-asiddha*), non-establishment of both, and that which is already established by agreement (*prasiddha-samāna*).
Among these, contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is, for example, saying "sound is not audible.
Contradiction with inference (*anumāna*) is, for example, saying "pots and the like are permanent."
Contradiction with one's own doctrine (*sva-śāstra-viruddha*) is, for example, as when the Vaiśeṣika masters establish that "sound is eternal.

Contradiction with the world (*loka-viruddha*) is, for example, as when it is said, "The hare-marked [object] is not the moon, because it exists," or as when it is said, "Human skulls are pure, because they are parts of living beings, just like conch shells."
Contradiction with one's own words refers, for example, to saying, "My mother is a barren woman.
Non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāprasiddhi*) refers, for example, to a follower of the Buddha establishing "the destruction of sound" against a Sāṃkhya teacher.
When the subject to be distinguished (*viśeṣya*) is not universally established, it is as when a Sāṃkhya teacher says to a follower of the Buddha, "The self (*ātman*) is volition (*cetanā*).

When both [the subject and the predicate] are not universally established, it is as when a Vaiśeṣika teacher establishes before a follower of the Buddha that "the self is the cause of conjunction (*saṃyoga*)."
That which is already established by common consensus (*prasiddha*) is, for example, saying "sound is audible.

Such numerous statements are called fallacies of the thesis (*pratijñā-doṣa*) because they function as a door to exclude the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, because they cannot be established [as something new], and because establishing them would be fruitless.
The fallacies of the thesis have already been explained; now the fallacies of the reason (hetvābhāsa) shall be explained.
The unestablished (asiddha), the inconclusive (anaikāntika), and the contradictory (viruddha) are called fallacies of the reason.
There are four types of the unestablished:
1. Non-establishment for both parties;
2. Non-establishment for one party;
3. Non-establishment due to doubt.
Fourth, the non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).
For example, in establishing that "sound is impermanent" and so forth, if one were to state, "because it has the nature of being visible to the eye," this would be unestablished for both parties.

Regarding "because it is a product" (*kṛtakatvāt*), for the proponent of the theory that sound is manifest (*abhivyaktivādin*), this reason is unestablished for at least one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*).

When there is doubt regarding the nature of mist and the like, if something is stated to establish the "presence of fire as a combination of the great elements" (*mahābhūtasamghāta*), this is unestablished due to uncertainty (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*).
"Space is substantially existent because it is the substratum of qualities. Against those who deny the existence of space, this reason for its substratum is unestablished.
There are six types of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*):
first, the common (*sādhāraṇa*).
2. The uncommon [reason];
3. that which occurs in one part of the similar class and pervades the dissimilar class;
4. that which occurs in one part of the dissimilar class and pervades the similar class.
5. That which functions as only one part of both [reasons];
6. Contradictory Determinants (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).
Among these, an example of "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) is: "Sound is eternal, because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatvāt*)."
Since both the permanent and the impermanent share this same reason, it is inconclusive:
Is sound impermanent because it possesses the property of being an object of cognition, like a jar and so forth?
Or is sound permanent because it possesses the property of being an object of cognition, like space and so forth?

Regarding the term "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*): for example, if one says, "Sound is eternal, because it has the nature of being audible," this reason is absent from both the class of the eternal and the class of the non-eternal; since nothing else exists outside of the eternal and the non-eternal, it is a reason of doubt (*saṃśaya-hetu*).
What is the nature of this "perceived property" (*śrāvaṇatva*)?

It is that which applies to one part of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) but pervades the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), as in the statement: "Sound is not produced immediately after volitional effort, because it is impermanent."
In this context, for the thesis that is not produced by immediate effort (*aprayatnānantarīyaka*), lightning, space, and so forth serve as its similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
This property of impermanence exists in lightning and so forth, but does not exist in space and so forth.
The thesis that "it is not produced by uninterrupted effort" takes jars and the like as its dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), and [the reason] is present in all of them.
Since this reason shares the same property with lightning and jars alike, it is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Is it because they possess impermanence like that of a jar and such things that they are produced by immediate effort?
Or is it because they possess impermanence like that of lightning and such things that they are not produced by immediate effort?

That which occurs in one part of the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) and occurs throughout the similar class (sapakṣa) is, for example, as when a thesis is stated: "Sound is produced by immediate effort, because it is impermanent."
The thesis produced by diligent and uninterrupted effort takes such things as a jar as its similar class (*sapakṣa*), and the property of impermanence is present throughout this class;
it takes such things as lightning and space as its dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), and within that class, the property exists in one part—such as lightning—and is absent in another part—such as space.
Therefore, as previously stated, this too is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Regarding that which "occurs in one part of both similar and dissimilar instances": for example, it is said, "Sound is eternal, because it lacks material resistance.

Here, the thesis (*pakṣa*) of eternity takes space (*ākāśa*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth, as its similar instances (*sapakṣa*). The property of lacking material resistance exists in space and the like, but does not exist in atoms and the like.
Taking things such as jars as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), [the reason] exists in pleasure and so forth, but does not exist in jars and so forth.
Therefore, because this reason shares the same property with both pleasure and emptiness, it is also called "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).

Regarding the "contradictory certainty" (*viruddhavyabhicārin*): for example, one might establish the thesis, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot," while another establishes, "Sound is permanent because it is audible, like the nature of sound."
Since both of these are causes for doubt, they are both termed "indefinite" (anaikāntika).
There are four types of contradictory [reasons]:

namely, the contradictory reason regarding the intrinsic nature of the property (dharma-svabhāva-viruddha-hetu), the contradictory reason regarding a specific qualification of the property (dharma-viśeṣa-viruddha-hetu), the contradictory reason regarding the intrinsic nature of the locus (dharmin-svarūpa-viruddha-hetu), and the contradictory reason regarding a specific qualification of the locus (dharmin-viśeṣa-viruddha-hetu), and so forth.

Among these, a reason that contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property (*dharma*) is, for example, stating: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced, or because it is emitted immediately following volitional effort."
This reason exists only in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa); therefore, it is contradictory.

An example of a reason that contradicts a specific property of the subject (dharmaviśeṣaviruddhahetu) is as follows: "The eyes and so forth must exist for the sake of another, because they are composite in nature, like bedding and other such things."

Just as this reason can establish that the eyes and so forth must exist for the sake of another, it likewise establishes the contradictory specific characteristic of the property to be proven—that they exist for the sake of a composite—because bedding and such things are utilized by a composite other [than themselves].

Regarding a reason that contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a property: for example, it is said, "Existence (*sattā*) is not a substance, nor a quality, nor an action, because it possesses [the universal] existence, and because qualities and actions possess [existence], just like the nature of generality (*sāmānyatva*)."
Just as this reason can establish the negation of substantiality (*dravya*) and so forth, it can likewise establish the negation of existence (*sattva*), because both are equally certain.

Regarding the "reason that contradicts a qualification of the subject" (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddha-hetu*): for instance, this very same reason, when applied to a qualification of the subject in the aforementioned thesis, establishes the nature of being an object of cognition (*ālambanatva*) while simultaneously establishing its opposite—the nature of not being an object of cognition—just as in the case of negating substantiality and so forth, because both are equally certain.
The fallacious reasons have already been explained; now the fallacious examples shall be explained.
There are five types of fallacious examples based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*):
first, the non-establishment of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma-asiddha*).
2. The thesis to be established is unestablished;
3. Both [the reason and the example] are unestablished;
4. There is no synthesis.
5. Inverted Combination.
There are also five types of fallacious dissimilar examples (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*):
first, that which does not exclude the probandum (*sādhya*).
2. Not excluding the probans;
3. Not excluding both;
4. Not being separate.
5. Deviation through inversion (*viparyaya-vyatireka*).
An example where the property to be established (*sādhya-dharma*) is not established is as follows:
"Sound is eternal because it lacks resistance; whatever lacks resistance is seen to be eternal, just like atoms."

However, regarding those atoms, the property to be established—namely, their permanence—does exist, whereas the property that establishes it—namely, the absence of material resistance—does not, because all atoms possess the nature of material resistance.
Regarding the "unestablished nature of the probans" (*asiddha-hetu*): this refers to the statement, "like cognition.
However, while all cognitions establish that the property [of being] non-obstructive exists, the property to be established—namely, permanence—is absent, because all cognitions are impermanent.
Regarding the case where both are unestablished, there are two types:
existence and non-existence.
If one says "like a jar," both are unestablished in terms of existence.
If one says "like space," for those who deny the existence of space, neither [example] is established.

Regarding "no conjunction" (*asaṃyoga*), it means that there is no joining together in that place; rather, both the probans (*sādhana*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) appear simultaneously in relation to things such as a jar.
For example, it is like saying, "In the case of a jar, one perceives its being produced and its impermanence.
A reversed application (viparyaya-prayoga) refers to what should be stated as "Whatever is produced is impermanent," yet is instead stated in reverse as "Whatever is impermanent is produced."
This is called a fallacious example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).

Regarding a fallacious example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) where that which is to be established is not excluded: for instance, it might be said, "Whatever is impermanent is observed to possess resistance, such as, for example, atoms (*paramāṇu*)."
Because the permanence of the dharma established by atoms is not refuted—since they assert that atoms are permanent—the probandum of "lack of material resistance" is absent.
Regarding "the probans not being discarded": this refers to the statement, "as with karma.
It discards only the probandum (sādhya) without discarding the probans (sādhana), because it is asserted that all karmas lack material resistance (apratigha).
Regarding "neither being negated": this is said in response to those who maintain the existence of [intrinsic nature], stating that "[it is] like space.
This is because space does not negate its quality of permanence or its lack of material obstruction; for space is described as being permanent and as lacking material obstruction.
"Non-separation" refers to stating, "Like a jar, it is observed to have the nature of impermanence and the nature of resistance.
"Erroneous separation" refers to stating, "All things that possess resistance are impermanent."
Such statements resembling the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*udāharaṇa*) are not genuine means of proof (*sādhana*).
Furthermore, for the sake of one's own awakening, it should be known that there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
Among these, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) refers to that which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).

If there is correct cognition regarding objects such as form (*rūpa*), which operates by directly engaging with each [object] while being devoid of all conceptual constructions such as names and categories, it is therefore called direct perception.
Inference (*anumāna*) refers to the observation of an object by means of its various characteristics (*liṅga*).
There are three types of characteristics, as previously explained.
Based on these as causes, there arises a correct cognition regarding the object of inference, such as the realization that "there is fire" or "it is impermanent"; this is called inference.
Within the two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), cognition itself is termed the "result" (*phala*), because it is the characteristic of realization;
since it manifests as having a functional activity, it is also termed "valid cognition.
Conceptual cognition that operates differently from the object is termed "pseudo-perception" (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).

This means that for those possessing wisdom, the conceptualization of jars, garments, and so forth arises; because these do not take the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object as their objective domain, they are called "pseudo-perception" (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).
If various cognitions of fallacious objects arise preceded by a cognition of a fallacious reason, they are called "fallacious inference" (*tarka*).
There are many types of fallacious reasons, as previously explained.

When cognitions arise regarding fallacious objects of inference by taking those [fallacious reasons] as their cause, and are unable to provide correct understanding, they are termed "fallacious inference."
Furthermore, that which correctly demonstrates the faults of the proof (*sādhana*) is called "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*).

This refers to demonstrating the deficiency of the initial proof, the fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*), the lack of establishment (*asiddhatva*), the inconclusiveness of the reason (*anaikāntikatva*), the contradictory nature of the reason (*viruddhatva*), and the fault of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*); because such speech clarifies and instructs the questioner, it is named refutation.
If one expresses words that falsely reveal a flaw in the proof (*sādhana*), it is called a "pseudo-refutation" (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*).

This refers to: stating that a complete proof is deficient; stating that a faultless thesis (*pakṣa*) has a fault; stating that an established reason (*hetu*) is unestablished; stating that a determinate reason is indeterminate; stating that a non-contradictory reason is contradictory; and stating that a faultless example (*dṛṣṭānta*) has a fault.
Such discourse is called "semblance of refutation," for it cannot reveal the faults of another's position, as that [position] is without fault.
Let us cease this matter here.
Having briefly proclaimed these few words of meaning, I have merely established the initial orientation of the compass.
Regarding the principles and non-principles within this, they are subtly elucidated elsewhere.

*Postscript to the Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra*, Volume One. The *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra* is, in essence, the gateway for vigorous debate and the proclamation of tenets, for crushing the heterodox and manifesting the orthodox.
By discussing the illumination of reality,
clarifying and manifesting the principles,
and entering the words to reach the fundamental source;
It is precisely because it distances one from the heterodox;
as for those who discourse upon it, they compare the ultimate aims and examine the essential points of convergence.
In the past, when the auspicious signs responded at the Bodhi tree, this meaning was fully realized; when he ascended to prominence in the Deer Park, these teachings were fanned abroad.
The six heretical masters bowed their heads until their foreheads touched the ground and rolled back their tongues in submission; the ten seers entreated for their lives to learn the way home.

This was not because the celestial spirit’s brilliance had dimmed its radiance or because the waves of heterodox currents surged; rather, it was because those who shared in evil were so rampant and their followers so numerous. Thus, Vasubandhu propagated the great legacy of the past, while Dignāga compiled the remaining fragrance for future generations. They extolled the truth and eradicated error, smoothing over difficulties and resolving entanglements; such is the perfection of their divine merit, as detailed in other discourses.

There arose the Bodhisattva Tianzhu (Deva), a sagely being of transcendent caliber, who comprehensively investigated and minutely analyzed the teachings, continuing the legacy of his predecessors. He composed this concise yet profound work, adapting it to the needs of the times; he opened with eight gates to facilitate the two benefits, pruning away five divisions to establish the definitive three branches. Thus its meaning is simple yet manifest, and its phrasing is brief yet clear.
The eminent scholars of the West have long held him in profound veneration; were it not for one who has trodden this universal path, they would not be fit to participate in his lofty discourse.

The Emperor of the Great Tang, seizing the opportune moment to manifest his sagehood, has spread the golden mirror and set in motion the golden wheel; he has received the succession of the enlightened and struck the jade drum to harmonize the jade candle. He has extensively disseminated the profound transformation and meticulously compiled the eternal statutes; he has kindled the torch of wisdom to illuminate the city of darkness and launched the vessel of knowledge to ferry beings across the sea of suffering.

I, Xuanzang, a Dharma Master of the Tripiṭaka, possess a spirit of awakening that is clear and penetrating, and my rigorous discipline stands preeminent among the multitudes. I practice the fourfold diligence as if never reaching enough, and I look toward the three schools with a desire for inquiry. The eminent masters of the land of Han each excel in their own specialties; wherever my eyes fall, I must examine their subtleties, and wherever my mind receives them, I exhaustively explore their wonders.

Alas! The traces of the Sage are remote and vast, and the teachings of the Image-Period have declined; there has never been a time when I did not sigh at seeing corrupted texts or heave a great sigh while pondering doubtful meanings.
Gazing toward the Onion Mountains with lofty vision, I look forward to traveling afar to Vulture Peak.

Thereupon, braving dangers and facing perils, he sought out teachers and inquired after the Way; his travels led him to the kingdom of Kaśmīra in North India, where he encountered the great master of śāstras Saṃghayaśas, who resolved his doubts regarding the Eight Piṭakas and examined the definitive principles of the Five Vehicles.

The Master of Śāstras, seeing that his profound roots were firmly established by great principles, praised his long-accumulated virtues; he taught him only the subtle arts of Hetuvidyā (Logic) for those points not yet understood, and upon hearing the Sanskrit sounds, the doubts in his heart were instantly dissolved like ice.

Later, in the kingdom of Magadha in Central India, he encountered the Bodhisattva Śīlabhadra, who further expanded upon these examples, extending them by analogy and refining them with gentle elegance.

Thereupon, he visited the remains of all the deceased and thoroughly inquired into their remaining achievements; though he encountered those who were as stubborn as armored bellies, his eloquence was peerless, and he laid low the followers of heterodoxy like the wind.
Furthermore, by synthesizing these treatises, he propagated and transformed the world, so that great blessings and prosperity flourished.
It was completed on the sixth day of the eighth month of autumn in the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era, translated by imperial decree at Hongfu Monastery.

The śramaṇa Mingjun of Hongfu Monastery received the dictation and verified the text; the śramaṇa Xuemu of Hongfu Monastery verified the Sanskrit; the śramaṇa Xuanying of Dazongchi Monastery corrected the characters; and the śramaṇas Daohong of Dazongchi Monastery, Mingyan of Jishi Monastery, Huigui of Luohan Monastery, Faxiang of Baochang Monastery, Wenbei of Hongfu Monastery, Daoshen of Fajiang Monastery in Kuozhou, and Shentai of Xiyan Monastery in Puzhou, carefully verified the great meaning.

Xu Jingzong, Minister of the Household serving as Left Attendant-in-Ordinary, Duke of Gaoyang County, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness and Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, received an imperial decree to supervise the translation.

The Tripiṭaka Dharma Master, with an empty mind responding to all things, opened this profound gateway; its ocean of meaning is vast and seemingly without source, and its peaks of diction are so lofty they are difficult to gaze upon. The eminent scholars from distant lands together received his direct instruction, and the records of these profound chapters have been circulated throughout the world.

Being of dull wit, I have unworthily received the favor of your commendation; having been entrusted with the task of verifying the text, I have had the fortune to encounter this auspicious occasion. I venture to record these contemporary events to bequeath them to future generations, so that this sublime model and vast cause shall not perish in the ages to come.
